body.en: Statistics and probability constitute 5 to 7 questions on the ACT Math test. ACT questions emphasize weighted averages, the effects of outliers on center vs. spread, probability rules (addition and multiplication), expected value in games of chance, and counting principles (permutations vs. combinations).
body.ar: الإحصاء and الاحتمال constitute 5 to 7 questions on the ACT Math test. ACT questions emphasize weighted averages, the effects of outliers on center vs. spread, الاحتمال rules (addition and multiplication), expected value in games of chance, and counting principles (permutations vs. combinations).

label.en: Definition 7.1 — Measures of Center, Spread, and Transformation Rules
label.ar: تعريف 7.1 — Measures of Center, Spread, and Transformation Rules

body.en:
Core descriptive statistical metrics:
  • Arithmetic Mean & Weighted Average:
    \[ \bar{x} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n x_i}{n}, \qquad \bar{x}_{\text{weighted}} = \frac{\sum w_i x_i}{\sum w_i} \]
  • Median & Mode: The median is the middle value of an ordered list (or average of the two middle values if \(n\) is even). The mode is the most frequently occurring value.
  • Spread Metrics:
    Range: \(\text{Max} - \text{Min}\).
    Interquartile Range: \(\text{IQR} = Q_3 - Q_1\), representing the middle 50% of ordered data.
    Standard Deviation (\(\sigma\)): A measure of dispersion around the mean.
  • Data Transformation Properties (Frequent ACT Trap):
    Adding constant \(c\) to every data point: Mean and median increase by \(c\); Range, IQR, and \(\sigma\) remain unchanged.
    Multiplying every data point by constant \(k > 0\): Mean, median, Range, IQR, and \(\sigma\) are all multiplied by \(k\).

body.en: Conditional Probability, Bayes' Theorem & Robust Summary Statistics: For any two events \(A\) and \(B\) with \(P(B) > 0\), conditional probability restricts the sample space to \(B\): \(P(A \mid B) = \dfrac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)}\). In descriptive statistics, the median and interquartile range (\(\text{IQR} = Q_3 - Q_1\)) are resistant to extreme outliers, whereas the mean \(\bar{x}\) and standard deviation \(s\) are pulled strongly in the direction of skewness.

In descriptive الإحصاء, the median and interquartile المدى (\(\text{IQR} = Q_3 - Q_1\)) are resistant to extreme outliers, whereas the mean \(\bar{x}\) and الانحراف المعياري \(s\) are pulled strongly in the direction of skewness.

label.en: Theorem 7.1 — Probability Laws, Expected Value, and Combinatorics
label.ar: مبرهنة 7.1 — الاحتمال Laws, Expected Value, and Combinatorics

body.en:
Fundamental probability and combinatoric formulas required on the ACT:
  • Addition Rule (Union of Events):
    \[ P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B) \]For mutually exclusive events (disjoint), \(P(A \cap B) = 0\), so \(P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B)\).
  • Multiplication Rule & Independent Events:
    \[ P(A \cap B) = P(A) \cdot P(B|A) \]If events \(A\) and \(B\) are independent, \(P(B|A) = P(B)\), so \(P(A \cap B) = P(A) \cdot P(B)\).
  • Expected Value Formula: For a discrete random variable \(X\) taking values \(x_i\) with probabilities \(P(x_i)\):
    \[ E(X) = \sum_{i=1}^k x_i \cdot P(x_i) \]
  • Permutations vs. Combinations:
    Permutations (order matters, e.g., ranking, officer positions, assigned seats):
    \[ {}_n P_r = \frac{n!}{(n - r)!} \]
    Combinations (order does not matter, e.g., committees, group selection, pizza toppings):
    \[ {}_n C_r = \binom{n}{r} = \frac{n!}{r!(n - r)!} \]
  • Empirical Rule for Normal Distributions (68-95-99.7):
    \(68.2\%\) within \(\mu \pm 1\sigma\), \(95.4\%\) within \(\mu \pm 2\sigma\), and \(99.7\%\) within \(\mu \pm 3\sigma\).

body.en:
• Outlier Sensitivity (Mean vs. Median): The mean is heavily skewed by extreme outliers, whereas the median is resistant. If an unusually high score is added to a dataset, the mean increases significantly, but the median often shifts only slightly or not at all.
  • Expected Value (Net vs. Gross Payout): On ACT raffle or carnival game problems, read carefully whether the question asks for gross expected payout or net expected profit/loss (which requires subtracting the entry/ticket fee).
  • Mutually Exclusive vs. Independent: For mutually exclusive events, \( P(A \text{ or } B) = P(A) + P(B) \). For non-mutually exclusive events, you must subtract the overlap: \( P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B) \). For independent events, \( P(A \text{ and } B) = P(A) \times P(B) \).
  • Combinations vs. Permutations: Order matters \( \implies \) Permutation \( _nP_r = \frac{n!}{(n-r)!} \) (e.g. officer positions: President, VP, Secretary). Order does NOT matter \( \implies \) Combination \( _nC_r = \frac{n!}{r!(n-r)!} \) (e.g. committee, team, selecting toppings).
  • Missing Exam Score for Target Average: If a student has taken 4 tests and needs an average of 90 across 5 tests, calculate the total points needed: \(5 \times 90 = 450\), then subtract the sum of the first 4 tests.

label.en: ◆ Why It Works — First-Principles Derivation (Statistics & Probability)
label.ar: ◆ لماذا تعمل هذه الطريقة رياضياً — First-Principles اشتقاق (الإحصاء & الاحتمال)

body.en:
Why Bayes' Theorem & Principle of Inclusion-Exclusion Work: Any event \(B\) can be partitioned into disjoint intersections \(B = (B \cap A) \cup (B \cap A')\). By additivity of mutually exclusive events and the multiplication rule \(P(A \cap B) = P(B \mid A)P(A)\):

\[ P(A \mid B) = \frac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)} = \frac{P(B \mid A)P(A)}{P(B \mid A)P(A) + P(B \mid A')P(A')} \]

Similarly, in counting \(|A \cup B|\), summing \(|A| + |B|\) counts every element in \(A \cap B\) twice; subtracting \(|A \cap B|\) once restores exact cardinality: \(P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B)\).

\[ P(A \mid B) = \frac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)} = \frac{P(B \mid A)P(A)}{P(B \mid A)P(A) + P(B \mid A')P(A')} \]

Similarly, in counting \(|A \cup B|\), summing \(|A| + |B|\) counts every element in \(A \cap B\) twice; subtracting \(|A \cap B|\) once restores exact cardinality: \(P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B)\).

label.en: Worked Example 7.A — Target Average & Total Points Strategy
label.ar: مثال محلول 7.A — Target Average & Total Points Strategy

body.en:
Samantha scored \(84\), \(92\), \(88\), and \(78\) on her first four chemistry exams. What score must she earn on the fifth and final exam to achieve an overall course average of at least \(88\)?

Step-by-step Solution:
  1. Use the Total Sum Concept: For \(5\) exams to average \(88\), the required total sum of all 5 scores is:
    \[ \text{Total Required} = 5 \times 88 = 440 \]
  2. Sum the four completed exam scores:
    \[ 84 + 92 + 88 + 78 = 342 \]
  3. Subtract the current sum from the target total to find the required fifth score \(x_5\):
    \[ x_5 = 440 - 342 = 98 \]
Samantha must score at least \(\mathbf{98}\) on her fifth exam.

label.en: Worked Example 7.B — Expected Net Value of a Game
label.ar: مثال محلول 7.B — Expected Net Value of a Game

body.en:
A charity lottery charges \(\$10\) per ticket. There are \(100\) tickets sold in total. One winning ticket awards a grand prize of \(\$500\), two tickets award second prizes of \(\$100\) each, and five tickets award third prizes of \(\$20\) each. All other tickets win nothing. What is the expected net return for a person who purchases one ticket?

Step-by-step Solution:
  1. Determine the prize values and their respective probabilities out of \(100\) tickets:
    Grand Prize: \(x_1 = \$500\) with probability \(P(x_1) = \frac{1}{100}\).
    Second Prize: \(x_2 = \$100\) with probability \(P(x_2) = \frac{2}{100}\).
    Third Prize: \(x_3 = \$20\) with probability \(P(x_3) = \frac{5}{100}\).
    No Prize: \(x_4 = \$0\) with probability \(P(x_4) = \frac{92}{100}\).
  2. Calculate the expected gross payout \(E(\text{gross})\):
    \[ E(\text{gross}) = 500\left(\frac{1}{100}\right) + 100\left(\frac{2}{100}\right) + 20\left(\frac{5}{100}\right) + 0 = 5 + 2 + 1 = \$8.00 \]
  3. Subtract the ticket cost (\(\$10\)) to find the expected net return:
    \[ E(\text{net}) = E(\text{gross}) - \text{Cost} = \$8.00 - \$10.00 = -\$2.00 \]
The expected net return per ticket is \(\mathbf{-\$2.00}\) (an expected loss of \(\$2\)).

label.en: Worked Example 7.C — Expected Value of a Discrete Payout Table
label.ar: مثال محلول 7.C — Expected Value of a Discrete Payout الجدول

body.en:
A raffle ticket pays \(\$50\) with probability \(0.04\), \(\$10\) with probability \(0.16\), and \(\$0\) with probability \(0.80\). What is the expected value of one ticket?

Solution:
\[ E(X) = 50(0.04) + 10(0.16) + 0(0.80) = 2.00 + 1.60 = \mathbf{\$3.60} \]

label.en: Worked Example 7.D — Permutations vs Combinations in Committee Selection
label.ar: مثال محلول 7.D — Permutations vs Combinations in Committee Selection

body.en:
From a club of 10 members, how many ways can a President, Vice-President, and Treasurer be chosen, versus a 3-person committee with equal roles?

Solution: Ordered offices use permutations: \(_{10}P_3 = 10 \times 9 \times 8 = \mathbf{720}\). Unordered committees use combinations: \(_{10}C_3 = \frac{720}{3!} = \mathbf{120}\).

question.en: A data set contains the values: 4, 7, 7, 9, 12, 15. What are the mean, median, and range of this data set?
question.ar: حل المسألة التالية في (Statistics & Probability): A data set contains the values: 4, 7, 7, 9, 12, 15. What are the mean, median, and range of this data set?

solution.en:
• Sum: \(4 + 7 + 7 + 9 + 12 + 15 = 54\).
  • Mean: \(\bar{x} = \frac{54}{6} = \mathbf{9}\).
  • Median: The two middle values are \(7\) and \(9\), so \(\text{Median} = \frac{7 + 9}{2} = \mathbf{8}\).
  • Range: \(\text{Max} - \text{Min} = 15 - 4 = \mathbf{11}\).

question.en: A committee of 3 students is to be chosen from a group of 8 candidates. How many different committees can be formed?
question.ar: A committee of 3 students is to be chosen from a group of 8 candidates. How many dإذا كانferent committees can be formed?

solution.en:
Because the order of committee members does not matter, this is a combination:
\[ {}_8C_3 = \binom{8}{3} = \frac{8!}{3!(8 - 3)!} = \frac{8 \times 7 \times 6}{3 \times 2 \times 1} = \mathbf{56} \text{ different committees} \]

question.en: A bag contains 5 red marbles, 4 blue marbles, and 3 green marbles. Two marbles are drawn at random one after another without replacement. What is the probability that both marbles are red?
question.ar: حل المسألة التالية في (Statistics & Probability): A bag contains 5 red marbles, 4 blue marbles, and 3 green marbles. Two marbles are drawn at random one after another without replacement. What is the probability that both marbles are red?

solution.en:
Total number of marbles initially: \(5 + 4 + 3 = 12\).
Probability that the first marble is red: \(P(R_1) = \frac{5}{12}\).
Since it is drawn without replacement, 11 marbles remain, 4 of which are red.
Probability that the second marble is red: \(P(R_2 | R_1) = \frac{4}{11}\).
Using the multiplication rule:
\[ P(R_1 \cap R_2) = \frac{5}{12} \times \frac{4}{11} = \frac{20}{132} = \mathbf{\frac{5}{33}} \]

hints.en: Probability that the first marble is red: \(P(R_1) = \frac{5}{12}\). Since it is drawn without replacement, 11 marbles remain, 4 of which are red. Probability that the second marble is red: \(P(R_2 | R_1) = \frac{4}{11}\).

question.en: The scores on a statewide standardized test are normally distributed with a mean of \(\mu = 500\) and a standard deviation of \(\sigma = 100\). Approximately what percentage of test takers score between \(400\) and \(700\)?
question.ar: حل المسألة التالية في (Statistics & Probability): The scores on a statewide standardized test are normally distributed with a mean of \(\mu = 500\) and a standard deviation of \(\sigma = 100\). Approximately what percentage of test takers score between \(400\) and \(700\)?

solution.en:
Express the boundaries in terms of standard deviations from the mean:
\(400 = \mu - 1\sigma\)
\(700 = \mu + 2\sigma\)
Using the Empirical Rule:
Between \(\mu - 1\sigma\) and \(\mu\): \(34.1\%\).
Between \(\mu\) and \(\mu + 1\sigma\): \(34.1\%\).
Between \(\mu + 1\sigma\) and \(\mu + 2\sigma\): \(13.6\%\).
Total percentage: \(34.1\% + 34.1\% + 13.6\% = \mathbf{81.8\%}\) (or approximately \(\mathbf{81.5\% - 82\%}\)).

question.en: A bag contains 8 red marbles, 6 green marbles, and 10 blue marbles. If 1 marble is chosen at random from the bag, what is the probability that the marble is NOT red?
question.ar: A bag contains 8 red marbles, 6 green marbles, and 10 blue marbles. إذا كان 1 marble is chosen at random from the bag, what is the probability that the marble is NOT red?

hints.en: To find the probability that the chosen marble is NOT red, determine the number of favorable outcomes and divide by the total number of outcomes.
hints.ar: To أوجد احتمال أن the chosen marble is NOT red, حدّد number of favorable outcomes and divide بتطبيق total number of outcomes.

hints.en: Find the total number of marbles in the bag: \( 8 + 6 + 10 = 24 \) Find the number of marbles that are not red (the green and blue marbles): \( 6 + 10 = 16 \).
hints.ar: أوجد total number of marbles in the bag: \( 8 + 6 + 10 = 24 \) أوجد number of marbles that are not red (the green and blue marbles): \( 6 + 10 = 16 \).

solution.en:
To find the probability that the chosen marble is NOT red, determine the number of favorable outcomes and divide by the total number of outcomes.

1. Find the total number of marbles in the bag:
\( 8 + 6 + 10 = 24 \)

2. Find the number of marbles that are not red (the green and blue marbles):
\( 6 + 10 = 16 \)

Alternatively, use the complement rule:
\( P(\text{not red}) = 1 - P(\text{red}) = 1 - \frac{8}{24} = 1 - \frac{1}{3} = \frac{2}{3} \)

3. Calculate the probability:
\( P(\text{not red}) = \frac{16}{24} = \frac{2}{3} \)

Common Misconceptions:
- \(\frac{1}{3}\) is the probability of selecting a red marble (\(\frac{8}{24}\)), failing to account for the word NOT.
- \(\frac{1}{2}\) or \(\frac{3}{4}\) typically result from counting only one of the non-red colors or miscounting the total number of marbles.
